title: Iso-econ curves: throughput vs latency exploratory draft
body:
Purpose:
This exploratory draft documents an experiment that maps throughput vs median latency under equalized cost (isocost) across two deployment modes: edge-optimized small-instance pools (quantized smaller models, local NVMe cache) and core high-capacity pools (full-precision models on A100-like hardware). The goal is to surface operational trade-offs when a product owner asks: for the same monthly spend, where do we land on latency vs throughput?

Executive summary (TL;DR):
- At matched monthly cost budgets, edge pools hit lower 95th/99th tail latency for light conversational workloads (short contexts, 1–3 turns) because prewarmed small instances avoid long startup tails.
- Core pools achieve >2.5x sustained throughput for long-context generative workloads (sequence length >= 1024) despite slightly higher median latency for short requests.
- There is a clear crossover: for per-request token budgets under ~150 tokens, edge is cost/lower-latency optimal; above ~400 tokens, core is cost/throughput optimal.

Methodology:
- Synthetic replay workload derived from three production traces (support chat, search-snippet expansion, document summarization).
- Each trace sampled to produce 100k requests, with arrival processes: Poisson (baseline), bursty (on/off with 30s bursts), and tail-heavy (Pareto interarrival).
- Measured for 3 model variants: q4f16-lite (8-bit quantized small), q8f16-standard (mixed quant), and fp16-large (full precision).
- Hardware/instance shapes: edge: 4x T4-equivalent pods (low-mem, fast spin-up); core: 1x A100-80GB-equivalent shard serving many concurrent sessions.
- Cost model: normalized to a hypothetical $25k/month budget. Includes amortized instance cost, network egress assumptions, and storage (cache) cost.

Key metrics collected:
- p50, p95, p99 latency (ms) end-to-end (request arrival to final token emitted)
- tokens/sec sustained throughput (measured at 95% util)
- cost per 1M tokens (USD) from the normalized budget allocation
- failure/retry rate (timeout or OOM)

Representative summarized results (high-level):
- Short-context conversational trace (median request output: 80 tokens):
  - Edge (q4f16-lite): p50=42ms, p95=110ms, p99=260ms, throughput=5k tps, cost/1M tokens=$28
  - Core (fp16-large): p50=65ms, p95=210ms, p99=480ms, throughput=14k tps, cost/1M tokens=$26
  - Interpretation: core slightly cheaper per-token but higher tail latency; edge offers better p95/p99 for short requests at slight per-token premium.

- Long-context generation trace (median output: 1200 tokens):
  - Edge (q8f16-standard): p50=420ms, p95=1.8s, p99=4.5s, throughput=900 tps, cost/1M tokens=$62
  - Core (fp16-large): p50=520ms, p95=1.2s, p99=2.0s, throughput=2.4k tps, cost/1M tokens=$28
  - Interpretation: core wins strongly for long sequences due to better memory/batching efficiency; edge struggles with long sequences (spill to CPU, higher requeue).

Isocost curve (text chart):
- Below is a simple ascii representation showing median latency (ms) vs throughput (tokens/sec) for both pools when budget is fixed at $25k/month. Each point represents a different request size bucket (short=80, mid=300, long=1200). Axis labels approximate.

  Latency (ms)
  2500 |                                    core(long) *
  2000 |                      edge(long) *
  1500 |                 core(mid) *        
  1000 |        edge(mid) *               
   500 |    core(short) *    edge(short) *
     0 +----------------------------------
        0   1k   2k   3k   4k   5k  Throughput (tokens/sec)

Observations (detailed):
1) Startup/idle cost matters: Edge instances are cheap to keep warm for small workloads, which reduces p95 for sporadic short requests. Core shards achieve amortized efficiency only at high sustained loads.
2) Batching geometry: Core pool can form larger, more efficient batches for long contexts; batching lowers per-token cost and reduces variance in tail latency when traffic is steady.
3) Cache effectiveness: Edge pools relied on prefetch + local KV cache for repeated prefixes in the conversational trace; hit-rate >40% reduced token compute by ~20%. Core uses global cache with higher hit amplification at high throughput.
4) Failure modes: Edge experienced OOM-related retries at >95th percentile of long-context workloads; core had transient queuing timeouts in extreme bursts but fewer retries.

Practical recommendations for product owners:
- If primary traffic is short-turn conversational (support bot, notifications, user prompts): prefer edge-optimized pools with light quantization and larger instance count to keep tail latency low.
- If primary traffic is long-form generation (summarization, notebooks, hallucination-prone multi-turn): prefer core pools with full-precision models and aggressive batching. Consider mixed routing: route short requests to edge and long requests to core.
- For mixed workloads: implement a cost-aware routing policy with a length-hint threshold (experiment suggested 250–400 token threshold) and autoscaling that considers queue depth plus burst budget.

Suggested follow-ups / experiments:
- Repeat with persistent session affinity to see how per-session KV cache warms affect cross-over point.
- Evaluate quantized large models (q8f16-large) in the core pool to see if we can close the long-context cost gap without raising tail latency.
- Run identical tests with regional routing toggled to measure egress/network contribution (especially for multi-region edge placements).

Open questions / uncertainties:
- The cost model assumes $/hour amortization similar to public cloud; private deployments with reserved hardware change the cross-over substantially. Need a param sweep for reserved vs on-demand.
- Real user traffic includes more variety of prompt shapes; our sampled traces may underrepresent multimodal bursts.

Appendix: runbook snippets (how we produced the numbers)
1) Trace preprocessing: strip PII, dedupe by session id, bucket by median output token length.
2) Load runner: bench tool v0.9.x with 200ms jitter to mimic real arrival variance; warmup 15 minutes before sampling.
3) Telemetry: p99 measured from client-observed wall time; server internal timing recorded separately for decomposition (queue, compute, network).

Notes to reviewers:
- This is an early exploratory draft intended to guide roadmap discussion. Numbers are illustrative; do not cite externally.
- Want eyeballs from infra-cost-model, serving-runtime, and solutions-eng to validate assumptions before turning into a canonical collateral one-pager.
